source_text: Quippe qui rationem et legem criminum amore calcaverant euntes post desideria sua, quae ipsa conscientia, cuius vis est maxima, castigabat. Verum quia constabat etiam Prophetas propter iustitiam crebro mortis enituisse contemptu et plurimos pro magnis quibusque rebus dignitatisque insitae fulgore rutilantibus securo ad interitum animo cucurrisse, ne non singularitas virtutis Christi dilucidior eiusmodi esset exemplis, intulit Apostolus, per quod ostenderet caritatem et fortitudinem illius unico eminere fastigio. Assentior et ego, licet raro, licet vix, tamen pro rebus iustis et bonis mori elegisse nonnullos. Sed illis negotiorum dignitas, id est ipsarum rerum, pro quibus dimicaverant, claritudo periculorum temperavit dolorem; Christus autem nihil habuit, quod amaret in studiis impiorum, et pro his, qui erant propria voluntate deformes, non est aspernatus impendi; apparet illum omnium virtutibus antecellere, quia, etsi in tolerantia paucos, in causa tamen nullos potest habere consortes. Nihil igitur de eius munificentia desperemus, quia, si pro nobis mortuus est, cum adhuc essemus peccatores, multo magis iustificati nunc in sanguine ipsius salvi erimus per eum ab ira.
pass_a_gloss: Namely those who had trampled reason and law by a love of crimes, going after their own desires, which conscience itself, whose force is very great, was chastening. But because it stood that even the Prophets had shone forth frequently by a contempt of death on account of justice, and very many for any great things and those ruddy with the brightness of an inborn dignity had run with a secure soul unto destruction, lest the singularity of Christ's virtue not be more lucid by examples of this kind, the Apostle brought in that by which he would show that his love and courage stand out on a unique summit. I also assent that, although rarely, although scarcely, nevertheless some have chosen to die for just and good things. But for those the dignity of businesses, that is the brightness of the things themselves for which they had fought, tempered the pain of dangers; but Christ had nothing which he would love in the pursuits of the impious, and for these who were deformed by their own will he did not scorn to be expended; it appears that he excels the virtues of all, because, even if in endurance few, nevertheless in cause he can have no partners. Let us therefore despair nothing of his munificence, because, if he died for us when we were still sinners, much more, justified now in his blood, we will be saved through him from wrath.

lemmas.lexica: LS iustificatio; Blaise forensic making-just, not later system
LS exemplum; Blaise Adam as example not transmitter
LS peccatum=fault, error; Blaise Christian sin
LS voluntas=will, wish; Blaise moral will
LS ratio; Blaise use of reason required for sin

pass_b_english: For they had trampled reason and law through their love of crimes, following their own desires, which conscience itself—a force of the greatest power—rebuked. Yet the prophets too were known to have shone repeatedly in their contempt for death for the sake of justice. Many others had run toward destruction with fearless minds for great causes radiant with the splendor of their inherent worth. Lest examples like these obscure the uniqueness of Christ’s virtue, the apostle added something to show that Christ’s love and courage stand at an unmatched height. I too agree that some people, though rarely and scarcely, have chosen to die for just and good causes. But the worthiness of their affairs—that is, the nobility of the causes for which they fought—softened the pain of their dangers. Christ, however, had nothing to love in the activities of the ungodly, and did not disdain to expend himself for those made ugly by their own will. Plainly he excels everyone’s virtues: even if he can have a few companions in endurance, he can have none in the cause for which he endured. Let us therefore despair of nothing from his generosity. If he died for us while we were still sinners, much more, now justified in his blood, shall we be saved through him from wrath (Romans 5:8–9).

choices.why: Paul's iustificatio vitae; keep forensic making-just, not a later systematic slogan as default.
Adam as example to later sinners, Julian's alternative to tradux.
